title: Priv VPC IAM Binding Factory Terraform module and upgrade/drift playbook
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Create a reusable Terraform module ("iam-binding-factory") that generates least-privilege role/policy bindings for Private (VPC) deployments across AWS and GCP, plus an operational playbook for upgrading existing org policies and automated drift/health checks.
background_and_rationale: Current private deployment repos include ad-hoc, hand-crafted IAM roles and cross-account bindings. This causes inconsistent privileges, excessive rights, and slow upgrades. We need a parameterized module that: (1) standardizes role templates, (2) enforces deny-by-default patterns, (3) outputs audit metadata for Console, and (4) provides an upgrade path with automated checks. The module should support both AWS IAM and GCP IAM bindings and integrate into our Terraform CI pipeline.
acceptance_criteria: Module published to internal Terraform registry with semver tags
Reusable examples for single-account, cross-account, and service-account flows (AWS assume-role role, GCP service account bindings)
Policy templates support permission-scoped variables (resource ARNs, prefixes, dataset IDs) to ensure least-privilege
CI pipeline runs terraform fmt/validate, tflint, and conftest checks for policy best-practices
Automated health check (priv-deploy-iam-healthcheck) validates that required bindings exist and reports to Console telemetry
Migration playbook with staged canary rollout (3 accounts) and rollback steps documented
design_notes: Key design decisions: 1) Keep role definitions minimal and opinionated: runtime roles (GRPC/Serving), infra roles (autoscaler), and ops roles (admin/read-only). 2) Use template-based policy generation (HCL templates + JSON policy fragments) to avoid hand-editing. 3) Expose capability to opt-in to broader permissions via explicit flags (e.g., enable_batched_kms_access) rather than escalating by default. 4) State lock support: recommend DynamoDB + S3 for AWS or GCS backend + locking bucket for GCP; module will not manage the backend but will expose guidance and example configs. 5) Provide outputs that can be consumed by the Console onboarding flow to display policy coverage per deployment.

decisions: Use template-based policy fragments (JSON snippets) to allow deterministic least-privilege generation and easier review
Enforce explicit opt-in flags for wide-scope permissions rather than allowing broad wildcards by default
Include healthcheck lambda/cloud-function that validates bindings and reports results to Console (not part of module but shipped alongside examples)
Do not manage remote state backend inside the module; document recommended backends and provide example configs
Require security review for major version bumps to the module (security_review_required flag set)
Adopt conftest/OPA for policy-as-code checks baked into CI

risks_and_mitigations: Risk: Overly restrictive generated policies break customer deployments. Mitigation: canary rollout, feature-flagged opt-outs, and detailed dry-run output for customers
Risk: Drift between Terraform-managed policies and manually created bindings. Mitigation: scheduled drift detection via healthcheck and PR generation tool to reconcile differences
Risk: Cross-cloud nuance differences (AWS resource ARNs vs GCP resource names). Mitigation: keep separate provider-specific templates and integration tests
Risk: State-lock misconfiguration during migration. Mitigation: provide explicit migration steps to set up state backend with state snapshots and lock tests
rollout_plan: Phase 1: Publish module as v0.1.0 to internal registry and enable in internal test accounts. Phase 2: Canary rollout to 3 customer-like accounts with SRE + SecOps monitoring for 2 weeks. Phase 3: Gradual rollout org-wide with automated PR generation for repos that require manual approval. Include post-rollout audit at 30d. If high-severity permission issues found, run rollback recipe in playbook.
test_plan: Unit tests for JSON policy generation, integration tests using Terraform in ephemeral accounts (CI job spawns short-lived resources), conftest/OPA tests for policy anti-patterns, and e2e healthcheck run verifying drift detection. Add schematics tests for both AWS and GCP example flows.
migration_playbook_outline: Step 0: Inventory existing bindings (script: scripts/inventory_iam.sh for AWS and gcp_inventory.py for GCP)
Step 1: Create canary workspace and apply module in canary account with dry-run outputs (terraform plan + policy-diff report)
Step 2: Validate application behavior with healthcheck and tenant smoke tests
Step 3: Apply to staged accounts with approval gates in the Console (2 approvers: SRE + SecOps)
Step 4: Monitor Console metrics and run audit queries; if regression detected, follow rollback section
Rollback: Use recorded terraform state snapshots to revert to previous state; if snapshot not available, run manual remediation commands included in playbook
